title: useState & functional updates
objectives: Predict what repeated setState calls in one handler produce, given state is a per-render snapshot
Choose the functional updater form whenever the next state is computed from the previous state
Fix stacked updates that lose increments by rewriting setX(x + 1) as setX(prev => prev + 1)
Write a lazy initializer, `useState(() => compute())`, so expensive setup runs only on the first render

sources.title: React docs: Queueing a Series of State Updates
React docs: State as a Snapshot

questions.prompt: `count` starts at 0. One click handler calls `setCount(count + 1)` three times. What is `count` on the next render, and why?

options.text: 1 — `count` is 0 in all three calls, so each one queues "set to 1"
1 — React batches the three calls and keeps only the last one
3 — React queues all three updates, so they add up
3 — each `setCount` updates `count` before the next line runs

questions.explanation: In this render, `count` is a snapshot: 0, and calling the setter can't change it. All three calls compute `0 + 1` and queue "replace with 1", so the next render has 1 (react.dev, State as a Snapshot). "React batches them" is the tempting wrong reason: batching only means React applies all three queued updates in **one** re-render instead of three. It doesn't drop any — queue three updater functions, `setCount(c => c + 1)`, in the same batch and you get 3, because each one receives the result of the one before.

questions.prompt: When should you use the functional updater form, `setX(prev => ...)`?

options.text: When the next value is computed from the previous value
Only in async code — inside a click handler, the state variable is always current
Only when the state is an object or an array
Always — the direct form `setX(value)` is deprecated

questions.explanation: Reach for `setX(prev => ...)` whenever the new state is calculated from the old. It's essential when you queue several updates in one handler (the snapshot is the same for all of them) or call the setter later, after an `await` or from a timer, when the closed-over value may be stale. "Only in async code" is the half-truth: React does make sure the state is current at the start of each click, so one update per click is safe either way — but the three-calls bug above lives entirely inside one synchronous handler. Setting a value that doesn't read the old one (`setName(e.target.value)`) needs no updater, and the direct form is not deprecated.

questions.prompt: A component declares `const [todos, setTodos] = useState(createInitialTodos())`. How often does `createInitialTodos` run?

options.text: On every render — React uses the result only on the first render and ignores it after
Only on the first render — React skips the argument once the state exists
Only when the component's props change
Once on the server, never in the browser

questions.explanation: `createInitialTodos()` is a function *call*, and JavaScript evaluates call arguments before `useState` even runs — so it runs on every render, and React throws the result away after the first (react.dev: "React saves the initial state once and ignores it on the next renders"). Pass the function instead, `useState(createInitialTodos)` or `useState(() => createInitialTodos())`, and React calls it only while initializing. (In development, StrictMode calls an initializer twice and keeps one result, so keep it pure.)

prompts.prompt: Rewrite this increment so three calls in a row reliably add 3, not 1.
prompts.explanation: The updater `setCount(c => c + 1)` queues a function, and React calls it with the result of the update queued before it instead of the render-time snapshot, so stacked updates compound: 0 → 1 → 2 → 3. In your own code the parameter name is yours to choose; react.dev's conventions are the state variable's first letter (`c`), its full name (`count`) or a `prev` prefix (`prevCount`).

prompts.prompt: Make `createInitialTodos` run only on the first render, not on every render.
prompts.explanation: Pass the function itself (`createInitialTodos`, no parentheses) or wrap the call in an arrow. Either way `useState` receives a function, which React treats as an initializer and calls only while initializing. Writing `createInitialTodos()` hands React the *result*, which means calling it on every render.

snippets.question: You click the button once. What does `console.log` print, and what does the button show afterwards?
snippets.explanation: `setCount` doesn't change the `count` variable in the handler that's already running — that handler belongs to the render where `count` is 0, so it logs 0. The setter queues an update, and React re-renders with `count = 1`, which the button shows. (StrictMode doesn't double-call event handlers, so there's one log in development too.)

snippets.question: After one click, what does the button show?
snippets.explanation: Values and functions go into one queue, processed in order on the next render. `setCount(count + 5)` reads the snapshot (0) and queues "replace with 5"; the updater then receives 5 and returns 6. Swap the two lines and you get 5: the updater runs first (0 → 1), then "replace with 5" discards it. A plain value replaces whatever is queued before it; only an updater builds on it.
